intro: Long ago, children in England and America played bat-and-ball games on any open ground. A book from 1744 has a rhyme called "Base-Ball." A Massachusetts town banned the game near its meeting house in 1791. Every town had its own way to play, with bases wherever players put them.

Then clubs began to write the game down. The Knickerbocker club of New York adopted written rules in 1845. Clubs set the bases 90 feet apart in 1857. Writers like Henry Chadwick printed box scores, and leagues kept standings. Chicago and Illinois became part of this story, from the White Stockings of 1876 to the Rockford Peaches.

In this unit, you will learn how the baseball diamond got its measured lines. You will be able to name the papers that set its rules. You will tell a legend apart from a record. You will also see who was left out of the early books, and when doors opened.
bigQuestion: How did measured lines and written records turn many backyard games into one shared game of baseball?

title: How a Diamond Got Lines

chapters.title: From a Lot to a Diamond
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a game played many different ways on empty lots become one game with measured lines?

story.title: Jackets for Bases
story.kicker: Four friends mark a game with jackets, then find a field where the lines are already painted.
paragraphs: It is a warm Saturday in Chicago. Maya, Luis, Dev and Rosa find an empty lot behind the corner store. They have one bat and one soft ball. They have no bases. Rosa drops her red jacket in the dirt. "That is first," she says.

Luis drops his jacket farther away for second. Dev uses a flat cardboard box for third. A cracked piece of sidewalk becomes home. Nobody measures anything. Second base ends up much farther away than first.

They argue about the rules. Is a ball that rolls into the weeds still in play? Maya says yes. Dev says no. They settle it the way kids have for a very long time. They make a rule for today and shake on it.

On Monday, Maya's class walks to a park district field. The dirt is raked smooth. White chalk lines run out from home plate in a straight V. Four white bases sit the same distance apart. A sign lists the rules for using the field.
Maya stops and stares. "Somebody measured this," she says. Her teacher nods. "Somebody wrote it down, too. A long time ago, people had the same arguments you had on Saturday."
story.think: What changes when a game's lines are measured and written down instead of made up each day?

lessons.title: A Rhyme From 1744
lessons.mainIdea: A children's book printed in London in 1744 already named a game called base-ball.
reading: In 1744, a London bookseller named John Newbery printed a small book for children. It was called *A Little Pretty Pocket-Book*. It had short rhymes about games, each with a small woodcut picture. One rhyme was titled "Base-Ball."

The rhyme tells of a boy who strikes a ball and runs to the next post, then home. The book never gives measurements or a full list of rules. It shows that English children played a game with a ball, a hit and places to run more than 100 years before the Knickerbocker rules.

Other old writings name the game too. The English author Jane Austen wrote a novel in the late 1790s called *Northanger Abbey*. It was published in 1817. In it, a girl is said to enjoy cricket and base-ball more than books. Base-ball was an ordinary word for a children's game.

a novel by Jane Austen, written in the late 1790s and published in 1817, that mentions base-ball
a picture printed from a carved block of wood

lessons.title: A Town Rule in 1791
lessons.mainIdea: In 1791, the town of Pittsfield, Massachusetts, banned ball games, including baseball, near its new meeting house.
reading: In 1791, the town of Pittsfield, Massachusetts, built a new meeting house. It had large glass windows. Glass was costly. Town leaders worried that stray balls would break it.

On September 5, 1791, the town passed a *bylaw*. A bylaw is a rule made by a town. It banned several ball games within 80 yards of the meeting house. The list named wicket, cricket, football and baseball. People who broke the rule could be fined.

The old paper sat in a library for many years. In 2004, the historian John Thorn and others made it widely known. It is one of the oldest written American uses of the word baseball. It shows the game was common enough in 1791 to be a problem for a town.

words.d: a rule made by a town or a club for its own members or land
a building where a New England town met for worship and town business

lessons.title: Town Ball and Sandlots
lessons.mainIdea: Before written club rules spread, bat-and-ball games changed from town to town and lot to lot.
reading: In the early 1800s, Americans played many bat-and-ball games. People called them town ball, round ball or base ball. In England, a similar game was called rounders. Each place had its own habits. The number of bases, players and outs could change.

In New England, one version was later called the *Massachusetts game*. Players often used wooden stakes for bases. In New York, another version grew up. Players from two towns could meet and find they knew different games.

Later, city kids played on empty lots covered in sand and gravel. Each one was called a *sandlot*. A sandlot game used whatever was around for bases. Its rules lasted only as long as the players agreed. The word sandlot still means a pick-up game with no official field.

words.d: an empty city lot where kids played pick-up ball games; also a game with no official field
a New England version of base ball that was different from the New York game
an English bat-and-ball game with bases, older than written baseball rules

lessons.title: The Knickerbocker Rules
lessons.mainIdea: On September 23, 1845, the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club of New York adopted a written list of rules.
reading: The Knickerbocker Base Ball Club was a group of young men in New York City. Many were clerks, merchants and doctors. On September 23, 1845, the club adopted a written list of 20 rules. These are called the *Knickerbocker Rules*.

Some rules were about club business, like showing up on time. Others described the game. The bases were set 42 paces apart from home to second. A ball hit outside first or third base was *foul*. A game ended when one side scored 21 runs, which the rules called aces.

Alexander Cartwright was a club member, and his name is often tied to these rules. Historians say several members wrote them together. The Knickerbockers were not the first to play the game. They helped by putting their version on paper, where others could copy it.

words.d: the 20 written rules adopted by the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club of New York on September 23, 1845
a hit ball that lands outside the lines of play
the Knickerbocker word for a run; the first side to 21 aces won

look.title: The bases in 1845
look.text: The bases are set from home to second base at 42 paces, and from first to third base at 42 paces, all the same distance apart.
look.cite: Knickerbocker Base Ball Club, Rules, September 23, 1845, rule on the bases
look.prompt: A pace is one long step. Why might paces cause problems when two clubs try to lay out the same field?

check.q: How many rules did the Knickerbockers adopt in 1845?
check.why: The club adopted a list of 20 rules on September 23, 1845.

check.q: Under the 1845 rules, how did a game end?
check.why: The Knickerbocker game ended when a side scored 21 aces, or runs.

check.q: What do historians say about who wrote the Knickerbocker Rules?
choices: several club members wrote them together
Henry Chadwick wrote them in London
check.why: Cartwright's name is often tied to them, but historians say several members wrote them.

lessons.title: Games at the Elysian Fields
lessons.mainIdea: The Knickerbockers played on a rented field in Hoboken, New Jersey, called the Elysian Fields.
reading: New York City was growing fast in the 1840s. Open land in Manhattan was being filled with buildings. The Knickerbockers took a ferry across the Hudson River to Hoboken, New Jersey. There they rented grassy ground called the *Elysian Fields*.

On June 19, 1846, the Knickerbockers played a club called the New York Nine at the Elysian Fields. The New York Nine won 23 to 1. For many years, this was called the first game played under written rules.

Historians later found newspaper reports of games in the fall of 1845. So the 1846 game was not the very first. It is still an early recorded game. A rented field meant a club needed a fixed place, a fixed day and rules both sides knew.

words.d: a grassy park in Hoboken, New Jersey, where the Knickerbockers played in the 1840s
a game between two different clubs, not just members of one club

look.title: A ferry to the field
look.text: Picture club members in 1846 carrying bats and a ball onto a ferry in Manhattan. They cross the river to a rented green field in Hoboken. The other club is waiting there. Each side has a copy of the rules.
look.prompt: Why did the club need to travel to play? Why did both sides need the same rules?

check.q: Where were the Elysian Fields?
check.why: The Elysian Fields were in Hoboken, across the Hudson River from New York City.

check.q: Who won the June 19, 1846, game?
check.why: The New York Nine beat the Knickerbockers 23 to 1.

check.q: Why do historians no longer call the 1846 game the very first?
choices: they found reports of games in 1845
it was played under cricket rules
check.why: Newspaper reports from the fall of 1845 describe earlier games.

lessons.title: Paces Become Ninety Feet
lessons.mainIdea: An 1857 meeting of New York area clubs set the bases 90 feet apart and the game at nine innings.
reading: By the 1850s, many clubs in New York and Brooklyn played the Knickerbocker way. In 1857, they sent delegates to a *convention*. A convention is a meeting where groups make decisions together. In 1858, the group took the name National Association of Base Ball Players.

The 1857 rules made big changes. Bases were set 90 feet apart, measured with a tape, not paces. A game became nine innings instead of 21 runs. A side had nine players. Daniel "Doc" Adams of the Knickerbockers led the committee that wrote these rules.

Printed rules traveled by mail and in newspapers. Clubs in other cities copied them. By the 1860s, clubs from many states had joined the association. Ninety feet between bases is still the distance in the major leagues today.

words.d: a meeting where groups send people to make decisions together

words.w: National Association of Base Ball Players
words.d: the group of clubs, named in 1858, that set shared rules for base ball
one part of a game in which each side has a turn to bat; nine make a game

look.prompt: Why does a tape make it easier for two cities to build the same field?

check.why: The 1857 convention set the bases 90 feet apart.

check.q: After 1857, how long was a game?
check.why: The 1857 rules changed the game from 21 runs to nine innings.

check.q: What is a convention?

check.why: Clubs sent delegates to a convention to agree on rules.

lessons.title: The Doubleday Story
lessons.mainIdea: A 1907 report said Abner Doubleday invented baseball in 1839, but this is a legend, not documented history.
reading: In 1905, Albert Spalding asked for a group to find where baseball began. Spalding was a star pitcher who was born in Byron, Illinois. He had become a sporting goods businessman in Chicago. The group was called the *Mills Commission*. It was led by Abraham Mills, a former National League president.

The commission received a letter from a man named Abner Graves. He said that as a boy he saw Abner Doubleday invent baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839. The commission's report came out at the end of 1907. It named Doubleday as the inventor.

This is a *legend*. A legend is a story many people repeat that cannot be proved. The report used one man's memory from about 66 years earlier. Doubleday had died in 1893. He never wrote that he invented baseball.

words.d: a story people repeat that cannot be proved true
a group formed in 1905 at Albert Spalding's request; its 1907 report named Doubleday as baseball's inventor
an Army officer whom a 1907 report named as baseball's inventor; historians call this a legend

look.text: The best evidence available shows that the first plan of baseball was made by Abner Doubleday at Cooperstown, New York, in 1839.
look.cite: Final report of the Mills Commission, December 1907 (claim based on the letter of Abner Graves)
look.prompt: The report calls this the best evidence. What was that evidence, and why is it weak?

check.q: What did the 1907 Mills Commission report claim?
check.why: The report named Doubleday, based on Abner Graves's letter. Historians call it a legend.

check.q: Who asked for the commission to be formed?
check.why: Albert Spalding asked for the commission in 1905.

check.q: Why do historians call the Doubleday story a legend?
choices: it rests on one man's memory and cannot be proved
Doubleday wrote a book about it
check.why: The story came from one letter written about 66 years later, and Doubleday never claimed it.

lessons.title: What Historians Found
lessons.mainIdea: Records show baseball grew slowly from older games, even though the Hall of Fame was built in Cooperstown.
reading: Historians checked the Doubleday story against records. In 1839, Doubleday was a cadet at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point. That is far from Cooperstown. He later served as a Union officer in the Civil War.

Older papers tell a different story. The 1744 rhyme, the 1791 Pittsfield bylaw and the 1845 Knickerbocker rules all came before or apart from Doubleday. Henry Chadwick, a leading baseball writer, argued that the game grew from the English game of rounders. Spalding disagreed. He wanted baseball to have a purely American start.

The legend still shaped a real place. The National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum opened in Cooperstown in 1939. That was 100 years after the date in the legend. Doubleday himself has never been elected to the Hall of Fame.

words.d: papers, objects or records that show something really happened
the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum, opened in Cooperstown, New York, in 1939

look.title: Story beside record
look.text: Left side: a letter written in 1905 by an old man remembering a day in 1839. Right side: a town bylaw from 1791 and a club rule list from 1845, both written on the day they were made.
look.prompt: Which papers are stronger evidence about when baseball began? Why?

check.q: When did the Hall of Fame open in Cooperstown?
check.why: It opened in 1939, 100 years after the date in the legend.

check.q: What did Henry Chadwick argue about baseball's start?
check.why: Chadwick argued baseball grew from the English game of rounders.

lessons.title: The Pitcher Moves Back
lessons.mainIdea: The pitching distance was changed several times and reached 60 feet 6 inches in 1893.
reading: The distance from the pitcher to home plate did not stay the same. In the 1860s and 1870s, the pitcher threw from 45 feet away. In 1881, the National League moved the pitcher back to 50 feet.

In 1893, the league moved the pitcher back again. It set a rubber slab called the *pitcher's plate* 60 feet 6 inches from home plate. Pitchers had grown stronger and faster. The league wanted batters to have a fairer chance to hit the ball.

That 1893 distance has lasted more than 130 years. It is still in the Official Baseball Rules. The 90 feet between bases came from 1857. So the modern diamond holds numbers set in different years by different groups.

words.d: the slab of rubber the pitcher stands on, 60 feet 6 inches from home plate since 1893
the rule book used by Major League Baseball today

check.why: In 1893, the pitcher's plate was set 60 feet 6 inches from home.

check.q: Why did the league move the pitcher back?
choices: to give batters a fairer chance against stronger pitchers
to make the game end sooner
check.why: Pitchers had grown stronger, so the league gave batters more time.

check.q: Which group moved the pitcher to 50 feet in 1881?
check.why: The National League made the 1881 change to 50 feet.

lessons.title: A Plate With Five Sides
lessons.mainIdea: Home plate became a five-sided shape in 1900, and major league bases grew larger in 2023.
reading: Early home plates were often round or square. Some were made of stone or marble. By the 1890s, the rules called for a square plate 12 inches on each side. Umpires had to judge each pitch against the plate's edges.

In 1900, the National League changed home plate to a *pentagon*, a shape with five sides. It was 17 inches wide across the front edge. The flat front faced the pitcher. It gave umpires a wider, clearer edge to judge. That shape and width are still in the rules.

The other three bases are square canvas bags. For many years, they were 15 inches on each side. In 2023, Major League Baseball made them 18 inches. The league said bigger bases would help keep players safer when they reach the bag.

words.d: the five-sided base where a batter stands and where a run is scored
a flat shape with five sides

lessons.title: Diamonds for Kids
lessons.mainIdea: Little League, begun in 1939, drew a smaller diamond for children and opened to girls in 1974.
reading: In 1939, Carl Stotz started *Little League* in Williamsport, Pennsylvania. It began with three teams of boys. Stotz wanted a game sized for children. His diamond put the bases 60 feet apart instead of 90.
Little League grew into a worldwide group. The first Little League World Series was played in Williamsport in 1947. Towns across the country built smaller diamonds for young players.

At first, girls were not allowed to play. In 1972, a girl named Maria Pepe played for a team in Hoboken, New Jersey, and was told to leave. A court case followed in New Jersey. In 1974, Little League opened its teams to girls. That same year, it started a softball program too.

a final set of games that decides a champion; Little League's began in 1947

check.why: Stotz's diamond put the bases 60 feet apart.

check.why: After court cases, Little League opened to girls in 1974.

chapters.title: A Scorebook and a Diamond Plan
chapters.bigQuestion: How did writing games down and drawing fields on paper let faraway towns share one game?

story.title: A Pencil on the Page
story.kicker: On a bench beside a chalked field, a scorebook waits for the first inning.
paragraphs: It is a spring afternoon at a high school field in central Illinois. A fresh chalk line runs from home plate out to left field. On the bench sits a thick scorebook, open to a clean page. A yellow pencil lies across it.

Mr. Okafor, a history teacher, keeps score for the school team. He writes the date at the top. He fills in the two school names and the list of batters. Each batter gets a row. Each inning gets a column of small boxes.
A fifth grader named Jada is visiting with her older brother. She leans over the page. "Why write it all down?" she asks. "Everyone can see who wins."

Mr. Okafor turns back a few pages. There are last week's game, and the one before that. "People who were not here can read this," he says. "The other school will send its numbers too. Then the whole conference can compare."

He points to a folded paper tucked in the back cover. It is a drawing of the field, seen from above, with every distance written in feet. "The book tells what happened," he says. "The plan tells where it happened."
story.think: Why might a written record of a game matter to people who were never at the field?

lessons.title: The Club's Own Books
lessons.mainIdea: The Knickerbocker club wrote down its games by hand in books starting in the 1840s.
reading: The Knickerbocker Base Ball Club did more than write rules. From the 1840s, members also kept handwritten game books. After each game, someone wrote the date and the players' names. They noted how many runs each player scored and how many times he was out.

These books are some of the oldest baseball records in the United States. Some of their pages survive today in library collections in New York. Historians use them to learn who played, when and how often.

A game book turned a single afternoon into a lasting record. A club could look back at a whole season. It could see which members came most often. The books show that members often played games among themselves, not only against other clubs.

words.d: a book in which a club wrote down each game's date, players and runs
a written account that keeps facts after an event is over
the part of the year when a club or league plays its games

look.title: One page from a club book

lessons.title: Henry Chadwick's Box Score
lessons.mainIdea: Henry Chadwick, a New York writer, helped create the box score so newspaper readers could follow games.
reading: Henry Chadwick was born in England in 1824. His family moved to Brooklyn, New York, when he was a boy. He grew up knowing cricket, an English game that already kept careful written scores. In the 1850s, he began writing about baseball for New York newspapers, including the New York Clipper.

Chadwick helped shape the *box score*. A box score is a small table printed in a newspaper. It lists each player with numbers such as runs, hits and outs. A reader in another town can see what happened without being at the field.

Chadwick also wrote early baseball guides and argued for clear rules. He is often credited with using the letter K to mark a strikeout in a scorebook. He died in 1908. In 1938, he was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame. In his lifetime, many people called him the Father of Baseball.

words.d: a small printed table listing each player's numbers from one game
an English-born New York writer (1824–1908) who helped create the box score

lessons.title: Innings in a Grid
lessons.mainIdea: A scorebook page uses rows for batters and columns for innings so a whole game fits on one sheet.
reading: After 1857, a game had nine innings and each side had nine players. Scorebooks were printed to match. A page has a *grid*, which is a set of rows and columns. Each batter gets a row. Each inning gets a column.

Scorekeepers use short marks to fit a lot on one page. Many give each fielding position a number from 1 to 9. The pitcher is 1 and the catcher is 2. These numbers let a scorer write down who made each out in a tiny box.

A finished page shows the whole game at once. Totals at the bottom add up the runs in each inning. At the end, a scorer can copy the totals into a box score. Printed scorecards were also sold at ballparks, so fans could keep their own records.

words.d: a set of rows and columns that makes small boxes on a page
the person who writes down what happens in a game
a printed card or page for keeping score of one game, often sold at ballparks

lessons.title: Rules in Print
lessons.mainIdea: Cheap printed guides carried baseball rules and records to towns far from New York.
reading: In 1860, a New York publisher named Beadle began selling *Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player*. It cost ten cents. Henry Chadwick edited it. It printed the rules of the clubs' national association, along with club news and records of past games.

A small guide could travel by train and mail. A club in a new town could read the same rules as a club in Brooklyn. During the Civil War, from 1861 to 1865, soldiers helped carry the game to army camps and back to their home towns.

In the late 1870s, Albert Spalding began printing *Spalding's Official Base Ball Guide* in Chicago. It came out every year for decades. It printed the National League rules and a year of records. Guides like these helped one written game spread across the country.

lessons.title: Standings and a Pennant
lessons.mainIdea: The National League, begun in 1876, kept a table of wins and losses to decide its champion.
reading: On February 2, 1876, club owners met at a hotel in New York City. They formed the *National League*. William Hulbert, who ran the Chicago club, led the effort. Eight clubs joined in the first season.

A league needs a fair way to choose a champion. The National League kept *standings*. Standings are a table that lists every club's wins and losses. The club with the best record at the end of the season won the pennant, a long flag that stood for the title.

Chicago's club, then called the White Stockings, won the first pennant in 1876. It finished with 52 wins and 14 losses. Albert Spalding was its star pitcher and manager. That club is the ancestor of today's Chicago Cubs.

lessons.title: Records Older Than the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Written records let Illinois schools compare results, and some records are older than the association itself.
reading: In 1900, Illinois high schools formed the Illinois High School Association, or *IHSA*. It sets rules for school sports and runs state championships. Before 1900, some schools already met to compete in track and field.

The IHSA keeps lists of past champions. Its track and field records name state champions from 1893, seven years before the association existed. Someone wrote those early results down. The IHSA later added them to its own lists.

Other sports came later. The IHSA's first boys tennis champion was crowned in 1912. Its first baseball state champion was crowned in 1940. Each year's results go into the same records, so a school today can compare itself with schools from long ago.

lessons.title: The Rule Book Diagram
lessons.mainIdea: The Official Baseball Rules include a drawing of the field with its measured distances.
reading: The Official Baseball Rules begin with the field itself. A rule called "Layout of the Field" lists the distances. It comes with a *diagram*, a drawing of the field seen from above. Builders can use it to lay out a new diamond.

The diagram shows bases 90 feet apart. The distance straight from home plate to second base is about 127 feet 3 inches. The pitcher's plate sits 60 feet 6 inches from home. Lines called *foul lines* run from home past first and third base.

The rules also set sizes for new major league parks. Parks built after June 1, 1958, must reach at least 325 feet down each foul line. They must reach at least 400 feet to center field. Older parks, like Chicago's Wrigley Field, were built long before this rule.

lessons.title: Chicago Builds Ballparks
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's major league clubs moved from wooden grounds to large parks built in 1910 and 1914.
reading: In October 1871, the Great Chicago Fire burned much of the city. It destroyed the White Stockings' ballpark and their equipment. The club did not play in 1872 or 1873. It came back in 1874 on new grounds.
Early ballparks were mostly wood, and many burned. In the 1900s, owners began building parks of steel and concrete. The Chicago White Sox opened *Comiskey Park* on the South Side on July 1, 1910.

On the North Side, a park opened in 1914 for a club called the Chicago Whales. It was called Weeghman Park. The Cubs moved there in 1916. In 1926, it was renamed Wrigley Field, after the club's owner, William Wrigley Jr.

lessons.title: A Scoreboard for Everyone
lessons.mainIdea: A big scoreboard turns the scorebook into a public record the whole crowd can read.
reading: A scorebook is small. Only the person holding it can read it during the game. A *scoreboard* is a large sign that shows the score to everyone in the park. It lists runs by inning, just like the bottom of a scorebook page.

In 1937, the Cubs built a large scoreboard above the center field bleachers at Wrigley Field. It is still worked by hand. Workers inside slide metal number plates into place as the game goes on. It also shows scores from games in other cities.

The same year, the club planted ivy on the outfield brick walls. Bill Veeck, a young club worker, helped with the project. Both the ivy and the hand-turned scoreboard became well-known parts of the park.

lessons.title: A Line in the Records
lessons.mainIdea: Black players were shut out of the major league records for decades, so they built leagues and records of their own.
reading: In December 1867, the National Association of Base Ball Players refused to admit the Pythian Base Ball Club of Philadelphia. The Pythians were a Black club. The association's committee said it would not accept clubs with Black players. This unfair barrier is called the *color line*.

Moses Fleetwood Walker played in the major leagues for Toledo in 1884. By the late 1880s, owners had pushed Black players out. Cap Anson, the star of Chicago's club, refused to play against Black players in those years.

In 1920, Rube Foster, owner of the Chicago American Giants, helped found the *Negro National League*. Black newspapers such as the Chicago Defender printed its scores. In 2020, Major League Baseball named the Negro Leagues of 1920 to 1948 as major leagues. In 2024, their players' numbers joined the official major league records.

lessons.title: Women on the Scorecard
lessons.mainIdea: Women played baseball from the 1860s, and a women's professional league played in Illinois from 1943 to 1954.
reading: In 1866, students at Vassar College, a women's college in New York, formed baseball clubs. Some people at the time said sports were not proper for women. The students played anyway, on the college grounds.

In 1943, many men were away fighting in World War II. Philip K. Wrigley, owner of the Chicago Cubs, started the *All-American Girls Professional Baseball League*. It played until 1954. Its teams were in Midwest cities.

The Rockford Peaches of Rockford, Illinois, played in the league for all of its seasons. They won several league championships. The league kept its own records and box scores. Most of its players were white; Black women were not signed by the league.
